transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you here today?

Well, I suppose I should start from the beginning, because it's been quite a confusing time lately. I live alone in my apartment, and I've been there for quite a few years now since I stopped working. It used to be very quiet, which I liked, but lately... well, that's really what brings me in today. I keep hearing these voices, very clear voices, and it's mostly when I'm in my apartment. But it's not just there. I like to visit the art museums downtown, especially on the weekdays when it's not so crowded, and I've been hearing them there too, in the empty rooms. 

It sounds like... well, it sounds exactly like a group of women whispering. And they're not just making noise, they're talking about specific things. They sound like they're right behind the walls, just whispering away. They keep telling me which photographs belong in the archive. They get very specific about the lighting and the composition, and they insist certain ones need to be archived immediately. I try to listen closely to figure out if it's the neighbors or maybe an audio tour at the museum, but the whispering just seems to come from inside the walls themselves, and it's always these women talking about the photographs and the archive. It's gotten to the point where I can't even enjoy the quiet anymore because I'm always waiting for them to start whispering again.
Have you used any drugs like cocaine, methamphetamine, or other stimulants recently?

Oh, no, no, absolutely not. Goodness, I've never touched anything like that. I mean, I hardly even drink coffee anymore because it makes me feel jittery, let alone... well, illegal drugs. I've always been very careful about what I put in my body, you know? Especially living alone, you have to be mindful. You can't just be taking things that alter your mind, not when you need to keep your wits about you. 

I remember back in the eighties, when I was working at the gallery, there were certainly people around who partook in those sorts of things—cocaine, mostly, it was very prevalent in the art scene then—but I always steered clear. It just seemed so chaotic, and I’ve always valued a clear head. Even now, with everything going on, with the whispering and the women in the walls, I know for a fact it's not because of anything I've taken. I don't even take over-the-counter cold medicine if I can help it, because I read once that it can cause strange dreams, and my sleep is fragile enough as it is. So, no, definitely no drugs, no stimulants, nothing like that at all. Just my regular vitamins, really.
Do you also believe the women in the walls are actually real and communicating with you?

Well, yes, of course they're real. I mean, why else would they be talking to me so specifically about the archive? But it's not just the women in the walls, Doctor. That's just one piece of it. It goes so much deeper than that. I am absolutely convinced—and I have been for months now—that the museum board, and probably the city arts council too, they've been monitoring my phone. 

I know it sounds like something out of a movie, but you have to understand the context. I have this archive, you see, a collection of photographs and documents from the Caribbean, things I've spent years putting together. And this archive... it's going to change everything. It's going to completely upend how the galleries tell the truth about that history. The established art world, they don't want that. They want the narrative to stay exactly as it is, neat and tidy and controlled by them. 

So they're listening to my calls. I can hear the clicks sometimes when I pick up the receiver, just this faint little click before the dial tone, and sometimes there's a slight echo when I talk. I've tried explaining this to my sister when she calls on Sundays, but she just brushes it off, says it's an old building with old wiring. But I know better. They know what I have, and they are terrified of it getting out. 

And you know, people try to tell me I'm imagining it, that the museum board doesn't care about a retired woman in an apartment, but no one—absolutely no one—has shown me a single shred of proof that they aren't monitoring me. If they aren't listening, why do the women in the walls know exactly which photographs I was just looking at? Why do they know which ones need to be archived immediately? It's all connected, Doctor. The board, the phones, the voices... they're all trying to control the truth about the Caribbean archive. And until someone can prove to me, with hard evidence, that my phone isn't tapped, I have to assume they are listening to every word I say. I even started leaving the phone off the hook sometimes, just wrapping it in a thick towel and putting it in a drawer, just to get a moment of privacy so I can think about the photographs without them knowing.
Did these voices and beliefs start after a new medical illness, head injury, or other change in your physical health?

No, no, nothing like that. I haven't been sick or injured. I mean, my physical health is perfectly fine, thankfully. I haven't hit my head or been to the hospital for anything. I've always been quite robust, you know? Even as a child, I rarely caught a cold, and I certainly haven't had any new illnesses lately. I go for my regular checkups with Dr. Evans—he's been my general practitioner for over a decade now, lovely man, very thorough—and my blood pressure is perfect, cholesterol is right where it should be. 

And as for a head injury, definitely not. I'm very careful. I don't drive anymore, so I'm not at risk for car accidents, and I always hold the handrail when I take the stairs in my building, even though there's an elevator, just to be safe. You can't be too careful, especially when you live alone and have such important work to do with the archive. If I were to fall and hurt my head, who would organize the photographs? Who would make sure the truth gets out? 

So, no, there hasn't been any change in my physical health at all. I feel exactly the same physically as I did five, ten years ago. It's just... the situation around me has changed. The museum board's interference, the women whispering in the walls... those things started happening, but it wasn't triggered by a fever or a bump on the head or anything medical. It's just that the stakes with the archive have gotten higher, and they know it, and that's why all of this is happening now. But physically? No, I'm as healthy as a horse, as my father used to say.
Are you feeling confused or disoriented about where you are or what day it is?

Oh, no, no, not at all. I know exactly where I am. I'm right here in your office, at the clinic, and it's Tuesday. The 14th, I believe. Yes, Tuesday the 14th. I always keep very close track of the days, Doctor. You have to, you see, when you're managing a project as significant as the archive. Every day has a purpose, a schedule. Mondays I review the sepia prints from the 1920s, Tuesdays—well, today I had this appointment, but usually Tuesdays are for cross-referencing the shipping manifests with the portrait dates. 

So, my mind is perfectly sharp. I'm not confused in the slightest. I know some people my age start to get a bit... foggy, I suppose, forgetting where they put their keys or what year it is, but my memory is like a steel trap. It has to be. If I were confused, how could I possibly keep track of all the connections? How could I remember which photographs the women in the walls told me to hide from the museum board? 

I know exactly what's happening around me, perhaps even more clearly than most people. I see the patterns, the connections that others just walk right past. Like the way the light hits the dust motes in my apartment at exactly 3:15 PM—that's when the clicking on the phone usually starts, by the way. It's all very precise, very orchestrated. So no, no confusion here. I am completely oriented. I know who I am, where I am, what day it is, and exactly what the stakes are. I just wish everyone else could see things as clearly as I do. It would make all of this so much easier if people just understood the reality of the situation instead of asking if I'm confused.
Have you had a time when you felt unusually elevated, energized, or needed much less sleep than usual?

Oh, sleep? Who has time for sleep when there is so much work to uncover? Yes, there are days—well, sometimes weeks, really—where I hardly sleep at all. Maybe I'll rest my eyes for an hour or two just sitting upright in my armchair, but I don't feel tired. Not in the slightest. I get these days when I just feel... radiant. That's the only word for it, really. Radiant and chosen. It's as if a brilliant light has been switched on inside my mind, illuminating all the hidden connections in the archive, and I know, I know deep in my very bones, that I am the only one who can do this work. The women in the walls tell me as much, they say I've been specifically selected for this exact purpose. The energy just courses through me, a physical warmth, and I can cross-reference the photographs and the shipping manifests for forty-eight hours straight without even needing to stop for a cup of tea. It's a magnificent feeling, Doctor, truly magnificent to be so perfectly aligned with your life's purpose. 

But... well, the problem is other people. They simply don't understand the urgency of it all. My sister will call—assuming the line isn't too heavily compromised by the museum board that day—and she'll tell me I'm doing too much. She'll use that patronizing tone and say, "You need to rest, you need to slow down, you're getting entirely too wrapped up in those old boxes." And Doctor, I can't even begin to describe the anger that bubbles up inside me when she says that. If someone questions my plan, or tells me to slow down when I am on the verge of a massive historical breakthrough, I become absolutely furious. Furious! 

It's not just a mild annoyance, it's a deep, blinding rage, because it feels as if they are trying to erase me. That's exactly what it is. They want to erase my work, erase my purpose, just sweep me under the rug so the established art world can keep their tidy, fabricated little narrative intact. How can I sleep, how can I possibly slow down, when they are actively trying to silence the truth? They just want to extinguish that radiant feeling, to make me small and quiet and forgettable, and I won't let them. I simply cannot let them. So yes, I get very energized, incredibly so, but the fury... the fury is just as strong, if not stronger, when anyone tries to stand in my way or tell me my work isn't the most important thing in the world.
Have you noticed yourself becoming more socially withdrawn or less able to take care of day-to-day tasks than you used to be?

Well... it's strange that you ask that, because yes. Yes, I suppose I have, but it's quite difficult to explain, especially after just telling you about how radiant and energized I feel when I'm working on the archive. Because there is another side to it. 

There are these... these terribly long stretches where all of that fire just vanishes. It completely drains out of me, like someone pulled a plug at the bottom of my feet. During those times, I'll find myself just sitting at my kitchen table. Just sitting there, staring straight ahead for hours on end. I have a row of little herb pots lined up on the windowsill—sweet basil, some thyme, a lovely little rosemary bush I bought at the farmer's market—and I will literally just sit there and watch them dry out. I know they need water. The little copper watering can is sitting right next to them, practically at arm's length, but I just... I can't seem to bridge the gap between knowing they need water and actually lifting my arm to do it. So they just wither, right in front of me, and I just sit there.

And as for other people... I completely shut them out. The phone will ring, and if it's not my sister or the museum board's interference, if it's actually a dear friend, I just let it ring. I don't call anyone back. I have friends from my university days who used to be such a vibrant part of my life, but I just can't muster the energy to engage. They'll leave voicemails—Eleanor called not too long ago, or maybe it was a few weeks ago, time gets a bit blurry during these stretches—and she invited me to a chamber music concert. I used to absolutely adore chamber music. Or someone else will invite me to a new gallery opening downtown. 

In the past, Doctor, I would have been the first one dressed and out the door for a gallery opening. But during these stretches? I listen to the message and I feel absolutely nothing. Not a single spark of interest. It's like a heavy, gray blanket has been thrown over the entire world, muffling everything. I don't care about the music, I don't care about the art, I don't even care about feeding myself properly. I just sit at that table, looking at the dead leaves on the basil plant, feeling completely hollowed out. So, yes, I withdraw entirely. It's not even that I'm actively avoiding them, it's just an absolute absence of... of wanting anything at all.
Have the voices and beliefs ever happened when you were not having one of those energized or depressed periods?

Oh, I see what you mean. You're asking if the... the reality of my situation with the archive only happens when I'm feeling that radiant energy or when I'm completely drained, like with the basil plant. That's a very interesting question, Doctor, very interesting indeed, because I have actually kept track of this. As I mentioned, I am very meticulous about my schedules and my observations. 

There was a period—I'd say it lasted for several weeks, perhaps even a full month, right around the time the weather started turning brisk last year. I remember it distinctly because I had just taken my heavy wool coats out of the cedar closet, and the smell of cedar was lingering in the hallway. During those weeks, I wasn't having those magnificent, sleepless nights of endless cross-referencing. I wasn't feeling especially energized, and I certainly didn't have that grand, chosen feeling, nor was I furious with my sister. I was actually sleeping quite normally, getting up at a reasonable hour, making my morning oatmeal with a few raisins, and going about my day at a very steady, very ordinary pace. I wasn't hollowed out or depressed, either; I was watering my plants right on schedule. 

But... and this is the crucial part, Doctor, so please make sure you understand this... the situation with the archive didn't stop. Not at all. Even though my mood was perfectly level and quiet, I still heard the whispers in the apartment. The women were still there. I would be standing at the kitchen sink, just washing a tea saucer, completely calm, and I would hear them murmuring just behind the plaster, keeping me informed. And the phone! I remained absolutely, one hundred percent convinced that the arts people were still monitoring my phone line. Every time I picked up the receiver to check for a dial tone, I could hear the interference. 

So, you see, it doesn't matter if I'm energized or just having a quiet, ordinary week. The museum board's surveillance and the voices guiding my work, they are a constant reality. They don't just go away because I got eight hours of sleep or because I'm not feeling particularly radiant. It's a continuous campaign against my research, Doctor, and frankly, it's quite frustrating to have to constantly explain that their monitoring doesn't just take a holiday when my energy levels stabilize. I mean, if you were managing a historical project of this magnitude, you would realize that the arts people never sleep, even when I do, which is why I have to remain so terribly vigilant...
How old were you when you first started hearing the voices or becoming convinced that the museum board was monitoring you?

How old? Oh, well... I am sixty-four now, so I suppose I would have been sixty-three, since this all truly began to crystalize about eight months ago. Yes, it's been about eight months now. It certainly hasn't been a lifelong... situation, if that's what you're implying. I lived a very quiet, very private life before all this tremendous responsibility fell into my lap. 

But about eight months ago—I remember the timing quite specifically, actually, because I had just finished cataloging a particularly fragile set of silver gelatin prints from the 1920s. I had them all laid out on the dining table, resting on top of acid-free tissue paper, of course, because you simply cannot be too careful with the emulsion on those old photographs. One wrong smudge and a piece of history is gone forever. Anyway, I was standing there, holding my magnifying glass, and that was the very first time I heard them. The women in the walls, I mean. At first, I thought it was just the building superintendent doing some sort of pipe work in the adjacent unit, or perhaps the radiator acting up, but the murmuring... it was too distinct. It was too focused on my work. They were whispering about the exact shipping routes I was cross-referencing. 

And then, within that same week, really just a few days later, that is when the absolute certainty hit me about the museum board. It was the click on the telephone line, and the way my mail was slightly... bent at the corners, as if someone had hastily shoved it back into the brass slot after inspecting the contents. I just knew. I knew in my bones they were watching my archive. So it has been eight months of this constant, unrelenting vigilance. Eight months of knowing, without a shadow of a doubt, that people are watching my work and trying to intercept my findings before I can publish the truth. It feels like a lifetime, Doctor, it truly does, given the sheer volume of material I've had to protect and the emotional toll of keeping it all safe, but yes, chronologically speaking, it has been exactly eight months since the voices and the monitoring became a reality.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you were not depressed or elevated, but the voices or surveillance beliefs were still clearly present every day?

Well, I... I feel as though we might be going in a bit of a circle here, Doctor, because I believe I just explained this very thing to you a moment ago when we were discussing the cedar closet and my oatmeal. But to be absolutely precise, since you are now asking about a specific timeframe of at least two weeks and whether it was happening every single day... yes. 

Yes, as I was saying before, there was a period of several weeks—well over your two-week mark, really—when I was not especially energized or grand. I wasn't feeling that magnificent, chosen fire, and I wasn't hollowed out or depressed, either. My mood was perfectly level and ordinary. 

But during those several weeks, every single day, without fail, I still heard the whispers in the apartment. It wasn't just an occasional occurrence or a trick of the light. Every morning, I would wake up feeling completely normal, and the women would be murmuring right there behind the plaster, keeping me informed. And my telephone... I remained completely convinced, every single day of that period, that the arts people were monitoring my phone. I would check the receiver daily, perfectly calm, and the interference was always there. 

So, yes, I know I am repeating myself, but it is terribly important that you understand this: even when I am not elevated or drained, the surveillance and the voices are a daily, inescapable reality. They do not take weekends off just because my mood has stabilized, which is exactly why my vigilance has to be so constant...
Have you been taking any prescribed medications recently, including steroids or Parkinson’s medicines?

Medications? Oh, no... no, certainly not. I haven't been taking anything like that. Steroids? Goodness, no, I wouldn't even know what I would need steroids for. I don't have any sort of severe inflammation or asthma or anything of that nature. And as for Parkinson’s medicines... well, as you can probably see, my hands are perfectly steady. They have to be, don't they? You simply cannot handle delicate historical documents, especially the translucent vellum records or those silver gelatin prints I mentioned earlier, if you have any sort of tremor. One slip of the wrist and you've torn a corner off a primary source, and then where are you? So, no, my motor skills are completely intact, thank heavens. 

Actually, I am very, very particular about what I put into my system. I don't even like taking a standard over-the-counter aspirin unless I have an absolutely blinding tension headache from squinting at the microfiche files for too many hours. I prefer to manage my health naturally, you know, with a very strict, very clean regimen. I make my oatmeal, I drink my tea—Earl Grey in the mornings, steeped for exactly four minutes, and chamomile in the evenings—and I just keep myself in pristine physical condition. 

I suppose the museum board would be absolutely thrilled if I were bogged down with prescriptions, wouldn't they? If I were drowsy or clouded by some sort of heavy medication, my vigilance would slip, and they could just waltz right in and intercept my findings while I was napping. So I make it a point to stay entirely clear-headed. No prescriptions, no steroids, no Parkinson's pills, nothing of the sort. I rely entirely on a good diet and my own natural constitution.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when the voices or beliefs were not present at all?

A period of two weeks where they weren't present? No, no, absolutely not. I don't think you're quite grasping the sheer persistence of this situation, Doctor. Since this all began eight months ago, as I was explaining earlier with the silver gelatin prints, there hasn't been a single day—let alone a two-week stretch—where I have been completely alone in my own home. 

The women in the walls, they are always there. Sometimes they are louder, of course, sometimes it's a very urgent whispering right near the baseboards when I'm trying to cross-reference my shipping manifests, and other times it's more of a low, steady hum, like a hive of bees just behind the plaster. But they never go away. They never take a vacation. And the museum board certainly doesn't take a fortnight off from monitoring my telephone line and tampering with my mail. 

If I had two whole weeks of silence, two weeks where I didn't have to check the receiver for that distinct clicking sound or examine the corners of my envelopes for tampering... well, I wouldn't even know what to do with myself! I suppose I might actually get a full night's sleep without having to barricade the cedar closet. But no, that simply hasn't happened. Not for a single day, let alone fourteen of them. The vigilance is constant, Doctor, because the threat is constant. They know the magnitude of what I'm cataloging, and they simply will not rest, which means I cannot rest either.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when your mood was completely normal but the voices were still there every day?

Doctor, I... I must confess I am feeling a little bewildered right now. Are you testing my memory? Because I am quite certain, absolutely positive really, that we just discussed this exact same question a few moments ago. I know I am under a great deal of stress from the museum board's interference, but my cognitive faculties are perfectly sharp. But, alright, if you need me to repeat it for your notes, or if you're trying to see if my story changes, I will gladly go over it again. I want to make sure you have it written down correctly, because it's a very important distinction to make.

Yes, as I said before, there was a period of several weeks—well over fourteen days—where my mood was completely, utterly normal. I was not especially energized, I wasn't feeling grand or swept up in that intense, rushing fire I get sometimes, and I certainly wasn't feeling low or depressed either. I was just going about my daily routine, making my Earl Grey tea, sitting at my desk, feeling as ordinary and level-headed as anyone else on the street. 

But the surveillance did not stop just because my mood was stable. Even during those several weeks of feeling perfectly normal, I still heard the whispers in the apartment. Every single day, without exception. The women in the walls kept right on murmuring while I was trying to read. And my telephone... I remained entirely convinced, without a shadow of a doubt, that the arts people were monitoring my phone line. I would sit there, feeling completely calm, completely myself, not elevated in the slightest, and yet I knew they were listening to every dial tone and every breath. 

So you see, it doesn't matter how I am feeling in my own mind. The voices and the monitoring are a constant, external reality, regardless of whether I am feeling grand or just quietly drinking my tea. Does that make sense now, Doctor, or should we go over the timeline a third time?
Have you ever had times when the voices or belief about the museum board were present even though you were not having any elevated, irritable, or depressed mood symptoms at all?

Doctor... I must admit, I'm finding this a bit exasperating. We literally just covered this. Are you quite sure you're listening to me? I don't mean to be rude, but I am detailing a very serious, ongoing situation regarding the museum board and the women in my walls, and it feels as though we are going in circles. 

But yes, to answer your question again, yes. I have had times like that. As I just explained a moment ago, there was a period of several weeks—a distinct, clear period—where I wasn't having any of those mood symptoms you mentioned. I wasn't depressed, I wasn't irritable, and I wasn't feeling that grand, sweeping energy I sometimes get where I feel I can catalog an entire archive in one night. I was just... normal. Just sitting at my desk, drinking my Earl Grey, feeling perfectly fine and level. 

And yet, even then, the whispers were still there. The women in the walls didn't stop just because I was having a quiet, ordinary week. And the museum board certainly didn't stop. I remained absolutely convinced, because the evidence was right there in front of me, that the arts people were monitoring my phone. I would pick up the receiver, feeling completely calm, not agitated in the slightest, and I could hear the clicks. I knew they were there. 

So, yes. The voices and the beliefs about the board are present regardless of my mood. It’s an external reality, Doctor. It doesn't vanish just because I'm having a calm Tuesday. I really do hope you're writing this down this time, because I don't think I can explain it any more clearly than that.
During those times when you felt unusually energetic and needed very little sleep, did you ever become so unwell that you had to be hospitalized or could not manage your usual life?

Well, yes. Yes, I suppose you could say things became unmanageable, though I wouldn't use the word 'unwell.' It was more a matter of the sheer volume of my responsibilities clashing with the... the pedestrian pace of everyone else around me. When I am in one of those periods, when the energy is just rushing through me like a current and I barely need to close my eyes for two hours a night, I am so productive. I am doing the work of ten archivists. But the problem, Doctor, is that the rest of the world simply cannot keep up, and that is where the friction begins. 

It got to a point where... well, I missed several very crucial board meetings for the local historical society, because frankly, sitting in a stuffy room debating budget line items seemed utterly trivial compared to the cataloging I was doing at home. And then there were the bills. I completely forgot to pay my utilities for three months because I was so focused on cross-referencing the silver gelatin prints. I just didn't have time for mundane things like writing checks for the electric company. 

It escalated to the point where I completely lost the trust of my colleagues. They thought I was being erratic, just because I was working at a higher frequency than they were. I was trying to explain the connections I was finding, the absolute brilliance of the patterns, and they just looked at me like I was speaking Greek. And then... well, then my cousin Eleanor had to step in. Eleanor, who doesn't know the first thing about archival preservation, suddenly decided she needed to manage my affairs. She actually contacted one of the museum administrators—behind my back, mind you—and the two of them decided I wasn't safe on my own. 

They took over my calendar. They started managing my money, which was incredibly humiliating. I couldn't even go to public events or gallery openings anymore because Eleanor was so worried I would 'cause a scene' or talk too much about the monitoring. They treated me like a child, Doctor. So, yes, I suppose I couldn't manage my usual life, but only because they wouldn't let me manage it my way. They had to intervene because they couldn't understand the magnitude of what I was accomplishing.
When the voices or the belief about the museum board are happening, do they only occur during your high-energy or depressed periods, or do they also happen when your mood is otherwise normal?

Doctor... I... I really must protest. Are you quite alright? Or is this some sort of psychological test of my patience? Because I feel as though I am trapped in some sort of looping temporal anomaly. We have literally, just this very moment, discussed this exact parameter of my experience. I am starting to wonder if you are actually listening to a single word I say, or if you are simply reading from a standardized list of questions without paying any mind to my answers! 

But fine. If you insist on making me repeat myself, I will do so. Perhaps I should speak more slowly? Please, make sure your pen is touching the paper. 

Yes, Doctor. As I have told you, there was a distinct period of several weeks when I was not especially energized. I was not feeling grand, I wasn't feeling that rushing current of productivity, nor was I depressed. I was completely baseline. Normal. And yet, despite my perfectly ordinary mood, I still heard the whispers in the apartment. Every single day. And I remained entirely convinced that the arts people were monitoring my phone. Because they were! My mood being stable did not magically stop them from tapping my line, nor did it silence the women in the walls. The voices and the surveillance happen regardless of whether I am high-energy or entirely calm. 

Now, I have explained this in excruciating detail, repeatedly. Do you finally have what you need on this particular topic, or are we going to discuss my tea-drinking habits and the phone clicks for a fifth time? Because I really do have other things we need to discuss regarding Eleanor's interference, and we are wasting precious time going in circles.
Have the voices or the belief that the museum board is monitoring you ever continued for at least two weeks when you were not having any manic, depressed, or irritable symptoms at all?

Doctor, I... I am genuinely baffled. I am completely and utterly baffled. I feel as though I am speaking English, and yet you are hearing something entirely different. Or perhaps you are not hearing anything at all? This is exactly, precisely what I have just been telling you. We have gone over this. We have gone over it again. And now, here we are, for what feels like the third or fourth time, circling the exact same drain. 

But fine. Fine. Let me spell it out again, and I do hope you are paying attention this time, because I truly cannot fathom having to explain this yet again. 

Yes. Yes, yes, yes. Two weeks? Try several weeks. There was a very specific, very distinct period of several weeks—not just two, mind you, but several—where I was completely, perfectly, entirely normal. I was not having any of those manic symptoms you seem so fixated on. I wasn't feeling grand. I wasn't feeling energized. I wasn't irritable. I wasn't depressed. I was just... me. Living my life, drinking my tea, going about my day at a perfectly reasonable, pedestrian pace. 

And during those several weeks, when I was absolutely not having any mood symptoms whatsoever, the whispers were still there. The women in the walls were still whispering in the apartment. Every single day. And the museum board? The arts people? I remained absolutely, unequivocally convinced that they were monitoring my phone. Because they were! The clicks were still there. The surveillance did not take a holiday just because my mood was stable. 

So, for the record, and I do hope this is the final time I have to say this: yes. For several weeks, with no mood symptoms at all, I still heard the whispers, and I still knew the arts people were monitoring me. Now, please, can we finally move on? Because this repetition is becoming entirely absurd.
Have you noticed yourself becoming more emotionally flat or less expressive than you used to be?

Emotionally flat... I suppose... well, I wouldn't use the word 'flat,' Doctor, because that implies a sort of two-dimensional existence, and my inner life is always quite intricate. But I do understand what you are getting at, I think. Eleanor has certainly made her own uncharitable comments about my demeanor lately. 

There are these long, extending stretches of time where I just... sit. I will sit at my kitchen table—it’s a lovely, heavy oak table, usually absolutely covered in my cataloging notes and archival folders—but during these stretches, I just sit there staring at the grain of the wood. And my little indoor garden... I keep herb pots on the windowsill, you see. Sweet basil, some rosemary, a bit of thyme. They need regular tending. But I will just sit there and watch the soil turn to dust. The pots just dry out, completely wither away right in front of me, and I know the watering can is mere feet away on the counter, but I simply cannot muster the... the spark to get up and tend to them. 

And it isn't just the plants, Doctor. It extends to my social correspondence as well. The phone will ring, and I just look at it. I don't call friends back. I don't even have the urge to speak to them. People I have known for decades will leave messages, inviting me out to things I have historically adored. A chamber music concert downtown, or a new gallery opening—and you know how deeply invested I am in the local arts and historical preservation! But they will invite me, and I just feel... nothing. No interest whatsoever. No excitement, no curiosity. It is as if a thick, heavy wool blanket has been thrown over my usual passions, muffling everything.
